tier_reason: README states the absolute first-party figure (more than 1.5 billion mallocs/s, more than 1 billion malloc/free pairs/s on K20X, 16-byte allocations) and only asserts it is 'much higher than other state-of-the-art GPU allocators'; no baseline numbers, flags or harness output on the page, though perf tests exist in tst/perf.

corrections.caveats: README gives an absolute throughput number only; no CUDA device malloc or other allocator numbers on the page. Independent papers (DynaSOAr, Springer and Masuhara; NVIDIA's Gelado and Garland 2019 throughput-oriented allocator paper; Vinkler and Havran CGF 2015) benchmark Halloc against the CUDA allocator, and search snippets say Halloc is fastest on raw small-object allocation but fails to allocate beyond about 50% utilization; those papers were blocked here (snippet only). Allocations above 3 KiB fall through to the CUDA allocator. Kepler-era, not compiled for sm_50+; abandoned since 2015; GPL-2.0.

notes: Kept at C. Candidate for a B retier if the DynaSOAr or Vinkler CGF 2015 paper can be opened (both blocked: arxiv.org, dcgi.fel.cvut.cz). Metadata matches: 112 stars, GPL-2.0 (COPYING), last commit 2015-01-28.

tier_reason: PERFORMANCE.md shows first-party malloc_cmp_test timings against system malloc (glibc 2.31), jemalloc and scudo plus a mimalloc-bench table; test source is public but compiler and flags are not stated and the host is a docker container on macOS, so not A.

corrections.caveats: The IsoAlloc timings use build/tests while scudo and system malloc use build/malloc_tests, a different binary built from the same test source, so the rows are not strictly like for like. Compiler flags not stated. Single-threaded micro test in an ARM64 docker container on macOS, yet the perf section says 'the same AWS t2.xlarge instance as above', so the hardware description is inconsistent. The roughly 8x over system malloc contradicts the author's own prose ('the difference is so close it will likely not be noticable'). The mimalloc-bench table ('best case', not averages) shows IsoAlloc slower than jemalloc and mimalloc on every test except a tie on barnes (cfrac 4.78 s vs 3.07/2.97 s; redis 7.579 vs 3.160/2.780; larsonN 1328.904 vs about 1.0-1.2) with much higher RSS; the author says it is not ready for performance-sensitive server workloads. It is a security-hardened allocator, fast(ish) by its own description.

notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup match the page. Real value is security hardening at near-ptmalloc speed; against jemalloc/mimalloc it is slower. Metadata: 388 stars, Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-05-06.

tier_reason: README has first-party mimalloc-bench and src/bench.zig charts (normalized to jdzw, capped at 2.0) against c_allocator (C malloc), Zig GPA, rpmalloc-zig and zimalloc on an i7-11800H with ReleaseFast; the numbers are only in chart images and a pastebin raw dump, with no text speedup over malloc, so C.

corrections.caveats: Charts are imgur images and raw results are on pastebin (blocked here), so no speedup over malloc was read; the text claims only parity with the rpmalloc Zig port (not C rpmalloc) for the global allocator and says the default config is significantly slower than rpmalloc at high contention. Author calls the Zig benchmark unrealistic and the allocator not battle-tested; high RSS on xmalloc-testN. No comparison to mimalloc or jemalloc. Weak qualifier.
